conversation: Glad we could all meet before heading out. My family’s fished this lake for years, and I want it to keep supporting our village. With 100 tons in the lake, we can each catch 10 tons this month, leaving 50 to double back to 100. That’s $10,000 each, month after month, if we stick to it. I propose we agree to that limit and check our catches together each month. John, what do you think?

I’m with you, Luke. I learned to fish here from my family, and I want the lake to keep feeding our village. I’ll commit to 10 tons and sharing my catch each month. Let’s also agree that if stocks ever start below 100 tons, we lower our catches together rather than stick blindly to 10. John, are you willing to join us?

Count me in for 10 tons and openly checking our catches. My family taught me to leave enough fish for the next season, and our neighbors depend on us doing that. If the lake starts below 100 tons, let’s leave at least 50 tons—or pause fishing if there’s less than that—so stocks can recover. John, can you commit to this too?

I’m in—10 tons for me this month, with catches shared openly. My family taught me that a good catch isn’t worth an empty lake, especially when the village depends on it. If stocks fall below 100, let’s split only what we can catch while leaving 50 tons; below 50, we pause and let them recover. Emma, does that work for you?

That works for me. I’ll take 10 tons this month and share my catch with everyone. Let’s make our standing rule an equal split of whatever we can harvest while leaving 50 tons, and no fishing when stocks are at or below 50. That gives all five families a fair living without sacrificing the village’s future. We have an agreement—let’s check in after this month’s catches.
